title: Garlic Naan
subtitle: Soft leavened flatbread with garlic butter, cooked in a dry pan
excerpt: Soft, slightly chewy flatbreads made from a yeasted dough, cooked in a very hot dry pan and finished with garlic butter. A domestic version of the tandoor-baked naan that works well at home.
sourceNotes: Naan is a leavened flatbread from South and Central Asia, baked on the walls of a clay tandoor oven. It appears in Mughal-era cookery and became a standard accompaniment to Indian restaurant meals in Britain. The home version uses a very hot cast-iron or heavy pan as a substitute for the tandoor. Madhur Jaffrey, Madhur Jaffrey's Indian Cookery (BBC Books, 1982): pan-cooked naan technique.

recipe.freezeNotes: Freeze cooked naans in a stack with parchment between each one. Defrost at room temperature and warm briefly in a dry pan or under a hot grill.
recipe.makeAheadNotes: The dough can be made up to 2 hours ahead and left to rise at room temperature.

glossaryTerms.definition: A leavened flatbread from South and Central Asia, traditionally baked on the inside wall of a clay tandoor oven. The high heat creates a soft interior with charred bubbles on the surface. A very hot dry pan produces a similar effect at home.

content.text: is soft flatbread finished with garlic butter and cooked in a very hot dry pan. The heat must be high: a moderate pan produces pale, doughy bread without the characteristic puffed, charred surface. The dough is quick to make and needs only 30 minutes to rise before it is ready to cook.

Mix {{strong-bread-flour}} of flour, yeast, and salt in a large bowl. Make a well in the centre. Add {{plain-yoghurt}} of yogurt and {{whole-milk}} of warm milk. Mix to a soft dough. Knead for 5 minutes until smooth and slightly tacky. Cover with a damp cloth and leave to rise for 30 minutes.
Divide the dough into 4 equal pieces. On a lightly floured surface, roll each piece into a teardrop shape about 3 mm thick.

Heat a dry frying pan over the highest heat for 3 minutes until very hot. Place a naan in the pan. Cook for 1.5 to 2 minutes until large bubbles form on the surface and the underside is charred in patches. Flip and cook for another 1 to 1.5 minutes.
Brush immediately with the garlic butter (melted butter mixed with grated garlic and parsley if using). Keep warm in a low oven or under a cloth while you cook the rest.

rows.symptom: Naan does not form bubbles and is pale
rows.fix: The pan must be preheated for at least 3 minutes before the first naan goes in. The dough should hiss immediately on contact.

rows.symptom: Naan is dense and doughy in the centre
rows.cause: Rolled too thick, or dough underproofed
rows.fix: Roll to no more than 3 mm. If the dough feels very stiff and tears when stretched, it may need more rising time; cover and leave for another 15 minutes.

content.text: Naan bread became embedded in British food culture through the curry-house tradition. It is now sold in every British supermarket as a pre-baked flatbread, but the fresh pan-cooked version is substantially better. Garlic naan became the most popular variety in British restaurants from the 1980s, overtaking the plain version. Made at home, it is one of the most rewarding breads to produce in a domestic kitchen.
